qa_results.question: How does insulin resistance contribute to endothelial dysfunction?
qa_results.final_answer: Insulin resistance contributes to endothelial dysfunction through multiple interconnected pathways. HOMA-IR, a marker of insulin resistance, directly mediates the relationship with microvascular dysfunction. Insulin resistance is associated with increased levels of IL-6 and TNF-α, both of which contribute to microvascular dysfunction. Furthermore, insulin resistance is associated with VCAM-1, a marker of endothelial stress, and this association extends to C3a. Obesity, often linked to insulin resistance, affects biomarkers such as ADMA, C3a, C5a, and sC5b-9, and is also associated with the Inflammatory Endothelial Stress Score (IESS). The IESS is associated with microvascular dysfunction and predicts uACR progression. Complement activation, mediated by insulin resistance and metabolic inflammation through pathways including IL-6 receptor signaling and direct targeting of the endothelium, also plays a significant role in microvascular dysfunction. Alterations in the arginine/ADMA ratio, impacting nitric oxide bioavailability, further contribute to microvascular dysfunction. Specifically, insulin resistance is associated with changes in this ratio, and the arginine/ADMA ratio serves as a surrogate for microvascular dysfunction. These factors collectively contribute to endothelial stress and ultimately, microvascular dysfunction.

Obesity, often linked to insulin resistance, affects biomarkers such as ADMA, C3a, C5a, and sC5b-9, and is also associated with the Inflammatory Endothelial Stress Score (IESS). The IESS is associated with microvascular dysfunction and predicts uACR progression. Complement activation, mediated by insulin resistance and metabolic inflammation through pathways including IL-6 receptor signaling and direct targeting of the endothelium, also plays a significant role in microvascular dysfunction. Alterations in the arginine/ADMA ratio, impacting nitric oxide bioavailability, further contribute to microvascular dysfunction. Specifically, insulin resistance is associated with changes in this ratio, and the arginine/ADMA ratio serves as a surrogate for microvascular dysfunction. These factors collectively contribute to endothelial stress and ultimately, microvascular dysfunction.
